19877-jack-haydon-s-quest:
Jack Haydon's Quest is a school story of Rushmere School. Jack is prefect there and captain of the first fifteen. He walks swiftly out of the school gates one day. His leave takes him to Longhampton, three miles away. A day-scholar friend lies on the sick list there. The errand of friendship launches his quest in earnest.

School stories made prefects into knights of a small realm. Rugby, honor, and loyalty were their working virtues. A quest beyond the gates tests all three. John Finnemore wrote many such tales for boys. His schools run on fairness enforced by heroes. This opening is the genre in miniature. Readers of Tom Brown will know the country.
19967-beauty-and-the-beast:
Beauty and the Beast is the classic fairy tale, retold here anonymously. The merchant's family has fallen into poverty. With no servants, the girls must work hard, like peasants. The sons cultivate the fields to earn their living. All live roughly clothed and simply. That fall from wealth sets Beauty's story in motion. A stolen rose will carry her to the Beast's castle.

Jeanne-Marie Leprince de Beaumont's version shaped this tale for children. Her Beauty is virtuous, dutiful, and brave in that order. The Beast's courtesy slowly disproves his appearance. Generations learned the tale in forms close to this one. Its lesson, that worth hides under roughness, never dates. This retelling keeps the familiar bones clean.
20018-evenings-at-donaldson-manor-or-the:
Maria J. McIntosh wrote Evenings at Donaldson Manor, also called The Christmas Guest. Its frame gathers guests for Christmas evenings of talk and tales. A quoted review praises McIntosh's Woman in America warmly here. She has written a clever book, the Protestant Churchman says. It contains much good word and truth, the review continues. American ladies are urged to consider her thoughts carefully. The manor evenings continue that improving vein.

McIntosh was a popular Southern writer of moral fiction. Her Christmas frame lets stories teach without sermonizing directly. Donaldson Manor's guests debate conduct, faith, and feeling nightly. The format suits holiday reading by the fire. American ladies were her declared audience and market. The book shows domestic fiction's respectable power.
20022-sequil-or-things-whitch-aint-finis:
Henry A. Shute wrote Sequil in 1904 as the sequel to his Plupy books. Its narrator Plupy keeps a diary in cheerfully bad spelling. He has forgot whether it was brite and fair since his last diry, he writes. Anyway, it is brite and fair today; lots of things have happened. Beany's father is a policeman now, which makes Beany feel pretty big. Plupy warns Beany had better not say much to him anyway.

Shute, a New Hampshire judge, wrote the Real Diary of a Real Boy first. Its misspelled boyhood became a national delight. Sequil continues Plupy's schoolboy wars, pranks, and loyalties. The comedy lives in the spelling and the deadpan alike. Grown readers remembered their own diaries in his. These books are American boyhood classics of their decade.
20198-lavengro-the-scholar-the-gypsy-the:
George Borrow wrote Lavengro, subtitled The Scholar, The Gypsy, The Priest. Lavengro tells, in part, of Borrow's own wild and bookish youth. He learned Romani, roamed with Gypsies, and sold Bibles in Spain. Critics praise how such writers pour their whole selves into their books.

Lavengro blends memoir, tale, and talk on language, roads, and faith. Its hero drifts between scholars, priests, tinkers, and horse dealers. Few English books mix such worlds with so odd a charm. Readers get a classic ramble through words, roads, and Romani life. Borrow's own life, wild and learned, remains the book's true and lasting center throughout.
20860-the-butterfly-s-ball-and-the-grass:
Praise from the Pall Mall Gazette fronts The Butterfly's Ball and the Grasshopper's Feast. Children, it notes, may spurn fine new picture books for plain old Goody Two-Shoes. That charm of the old and homely sets this slight book's tone.

William Roscoe's verse ball of insects dates to the early 1800s. Butterflies dance, grasshoppers feast, and small beasts hold a gay ball. The poem ranks among the first true picture-book verses for children. Its light lines and beast pageantry paved the way for the animal picture books children still love today.
21033-sketch-of-the-mythology-of-the-nor:
Desert sands, furnace blasts, floods, and fire rivers scour the lands in this mythology sketch. John Wesley Powell opens his study of North American Indian myth with nature's vast force. Fruits shrivel before starved men's eyes as rivers rage and mountains burst.

Powell, who ran the Colorado River, led the Bureau of Ethnology's early work. This first annual report sketch sorts native myths by the powers they name. Sun, storm, beast, and hero tales take ordered place in his scheme. Scholars have revised his frame since, yet the sketch stays a landmark of the field's bold, early reach.
21133-true-to-his-colours-the-life-that-:
Crossbourne, a quiet village among hills, is the scene of the Reverend Theodore P. Wilson's tale of a sceptic's home. Wilson sets his story some forty years before he wrote, in a place that seemed to hide from the roaring traffic around it. A stream runs restlessly through the village day and night.

True to His Colours argues, in story form, for the life that wears best: steady Christian faith over drink and doubt. Long sermons run through the narrative, as Wilson's readers expected from his temperance fiction. The village cast works out questions of belief, drink, and duty in their daily rounds and troubles.
21298-the-black-tor-a-tale-of-the-reign-:
Two teenage boys from feuding families meet among the wild hills of Derbyshire's Peak District. George Manville Fenn sets their tale in the reign of James the First, their families locked in a centuries-old feud. Each lives in a castle above the moors. A band of ex-soldiers camps on the hills and descends to rob the poorer folk.

The boys form a secret alliance, gathering their fathers' workmen into a small private army against the raiders. Their first attack fails badly. With better weapons and a better plan they try again. Fenn sets honour, inherited hate, and common danger against each other, letting the feud's youngest heirs end what their fathers could not.
21311-gil-the-gunner-the-youngest-office:
Gilbert Vincent goes out to India as a very young soldier in George Manville Fenn's long tale of the East. Schoolboy fights open the book before the regiment sails. In India, battles follow in quick order, and Gil is wounded, knocked out, and recovering as often as he fights.

At one point a wealthy local rajah captures Gil and treats him like an honoured guest, offering him any jewels he likes. Gil refuses, saying freedom to return to his father in the regiment is worth more than gems. The fighting aims at pushing the British out of India, and Fenn follows its cost on both sides.
21313-in-honour-s-cause-a-tale-of-the-da:
Frank Gowan, seventeen, is a page in the Prince of Wales's anteroom at the court of George the First. His father serves in the King's Guard, while fellow page Andrew leans Jacobite, like his father. George Manville Fenn fills the Hanoverian court with German and Dutch courtiers the king brought for comfort.

A German baron deliberately insults Frank's father, and their duel leaves the baron badly wounded. Though loyal to the king, Sir Robert Gowan is sentenced to lose his regiment and leave the country. Frank's search for his father runs through rooftop escapes, spies, and disguises around St James's Palace and its park.
21378-yussuf-the-guide-or-the-mountain-b:
Lawrence, a consumptive boy in his late teens with no relations, wishes aloud for a holiday somewhere hot and sunny. His doctor and a retired professor agree to take him to Asia Minor to see the antiquities, under his lawyer guardian's eye. George Manville Fenn sends the party first to Greece.

Dishonest ship crews sour the start, though their luggage went safely ahead. In Turkey they hire Yussuf, a charming and resourceful guide, and travel inland as helpfulness thins town by town. Mountain bandits capture the party at last and demand a ransom. Yussuf's skill becomes their best hope, in Fenn's tale of sickness, travel, and escape.
21384-afar-in-the-forest:
A young settler tells the tale in W. H. G. Kingston's Afar in the Forest, a short novel of life in the wild woods. He hunts game for the family store while his Uncle Mark fells tall trees around their home. Bit by bit, the two clear land at their new place.

Much of the book is Uncle Mark's own story, told by the fire at night. He tells why the family left home, how they landed safe, and how they found an old settlement in ruins. Lost kin, hidden ties, and two rescued children give the tale its twists. Kingston keeps the cast tangled on purpose, so close reading pays off.
21464-the-gilpins-and-their-fortunes-a-s:
Two school leavers talk over their futures at the start of W. H. G. Kingston's The Gilpins. One Gilpin boy dreams, with his brother, of farming in Australia like their hard-working father. The brothers sail, and their luck turns on a Sydney quay.

There they save a family from a carriage with bolting horses, and win strong friends. The friends place them as overseers of a run-down sheep and cattle station past the Blue Mountains. The old manager was a crook, and many hands, sent out for crimes, are idle or worse. Mutiny brews before the brothers can set things right.
21493-twice-lost:
Godfrey Rayner's father, a half-pay naval lieutenant, joins a Bristol merchant house in W. H. G. Kingston's Twice Lost. The boy ships as a midshipman on the Heroine for the Pacific. There the tale's lost boy, Harry, first comes into view.

Islanders hold a shipwrecked sailor, and Harry proves to be an English boy used as a pearl diver. The crew takes him aboard and frees him from cruel masters. Years later the party settles in Australia, on the station next to Harry's own parents. Chance and grit drive this warm, tidy tale of loss and return.
21495-to-the-west:
Two young clerks quit a tyrant of an auctioneer in George Manville Fenn's To the West. They set their sights on British Columbia, far across the sea. The way there runs round Cape Horn to San Francisco, then up the coast.

On the road they meet folk good and bad, as Fenn's heroes always do. At last they reach the north and turn to hunting gold. Fenn draws places he never saw with striking life and care. The book runs long for him, some fifteen hours read aloud, and keeps its pace through storms, claims, and close calls.
21558-the-children-of-the-new-forest:
King Charles flees toward the New Forest as Captain Marryat's The Children of the New Forest opens. Marryat published the tale in 1847, his twenty-fourth book and the last of his lifetime. It was written for children and has stayed in print ever since.

When their father falls for the king, the Beverley children hide in a forester's cottage. They learn to farm, hunt, and live by their own hands. Roundhead foes and loyal friends test their courage and wit. The book's blend of history, woodcraft, and family love made it a lasting classic of children's fiction.
21676-confessions-of-a-caricaturist:
Oliver Herford confesses his art in Confessions of a Caricaturist, published in 1917 and dedicated to William Dean Howells. Short verses sit beside drawings of famed men, from Napoleon to Saint Paul. Herford likes Napoleon best, he says, since one hand hides in his vest.

Drawing hands, he owns, is not his knack, and Napoleon spares him the trouble. Roosevelt, Kipling, Shaw, Morgan, and Rockefeller take their turns in rhyme. Even Dante gets a joke about Benedictine and Chianti. Herford's light touch made him the wittiest pen-and-pencil man of his New York circle.
21734-the-golden-dream-adventures-in-the:
Gold in the far West draws the cast of this Ballantyne adventure across an ocean and a continent. The golden dream of the title is the hope of quick wealth that pulled thousands west in his century. Ballantyne knew the wild side of North America from his own years in Canada. He sets green newcomers against a land that tests every promise it seems to make.

The tale follows the party through travel, work, and danger in the western wilds. Greed, luck, and friendship pull the story in turn. Ballantyne keeps his moral steady: wealth found too fast can cost more than it pays. Young readers of his day took the warning with the adventure, gladly.
21753-the-norsemen-in-the-west:
Greenland eight or nine hundred years ago opens this Ballantyne tale of the Norsemen who reached America before Columbus. Two shaggy figures in bear-like dress creep over a ridge above a small hamlet of cottages, sheds, sheep, and boats. A sturdy settler plays with his small son outside the main cottage. The scene sets a whole lost world in motion.

Ballantyne follows the Norse settlers west from Greenland toward the new lands beyond the sea. Voyages, meetings with native peoples, and the hardships of a far colony fill the tale. He wrote it to give boys a true old story: that Europeans crossed the Atlantic long before Columbus. History and adventure sail in the same boat here.
21823-the-butterfly-s-ball-and-the-grass:
Tiny field creatures gather for a feast in this small book of verse by R. M. Ballantyne, published in 1874 for very young children. The gadfly blows his trumpet to call the company: beetle, emmet, gnat, and dragonfly all come in their colors. Predators lay aside their wars for the day and join the dance. A few over-eager dancers cause small mishaps, all safely mended.

Ballantyne wrote half a dozen such books for the youngest readers, some under the name Comus. This one is perhaps a twentieth the size of his sea novels. The rhymes are simple, merry, and meant to be read aloud. It shows the great adventure writer playing gently at the nursery door.
21871-adventures-in-the-far-west:
Young Britons cross the North American West in this short, picture-filled adventure by W. H. G. Kingston. Twenty-nine illustrations crowd the book, including a striking scene of a witch doctor visiting a sick man. The party travels among grizzly bears, wolves, and tribes who do not want them there. For much of the tale they live with a friendly tribe, whose ways Kingston describes at length.

Near the end, the heroes help rescue an emigrant wagon train attacked by a hostile tribe. A young lady has been seized and carried off, and the chase is on. Charley Fielding's cry at the campfire opens the action. Kingston's style, the editor says, is as excellent as ever. It is a brisk western in his classic mold.
22042-christmas-its-origin-and-associati:
William Francis Dawson set out to trace Christmas from its beginnings to his own day. His Christmas: Its Origin and Associations gathers customs scattered through many older authors. He found that some great Christmas feasts marked turning points in English history. He also saw the yearly feast as a link in the chain of Christian evidence across nineteen centuries.

Dawson moves from Roman and pagan roots through medieval revels to Victorian family practice. Holly, mistletoe, carols, feasts, and charity all get their histories. The book is earnest, well stocked, and proud of its subject. It suits readers who want the story behind the holiday's familiar trimmings.
22277-darry-the-life-saver-or-the-heroes:
Frank V. Webster wrote Darry the Life Saver, or The Heroes of the Coast, in 1911 for boy readers. Webster supplied many volumes to the cheap series trade under his own name and others. His hero Darry belongs to the surfmen who guarded America's coasts. The book opens on a brigantine battered by a Caribbean hurricane, staggering along like a wounded beast, her masts gone by the board.

From that wreck the tale builds rescues by breeches buoy and lifeboat. One picture shows a woman lowered safely and stowed away. The Life-Saving Service, forerunner of the Coast Guard, supplies real practice behind the thrills. Darry's adventures honour men who rowed out when others ran from the sea.
23094-the-boy-nihilist:
Allan Arnold recruits a bright young fellow in The Boy Nihilist. Friends knew his talents well. So did members of the secret societies scattered across Ireland, Germany, and Russia. They knew him as a bright young fellow with brains, pluck, and enthusiasm, which, rightly directed, would make him valuable to any secret organization having the people's liberty at heart.

Beyond that, nothing particular was known of him, which is exactly how dime novels like their conspirators. Plots, bombs, and disguises fill this entry in the era's anxious literature of anarchism. Arnold writes the secret-society scare as boys' adventure. The book survives as a period artifact, showing how 1890s headlines about nihilists were repackaged for young readers hungry for danger.
23155-western-characters-or-types-of-bor:
James Hall apologizes for a gap in Western Characters, his types of border life in the western states. A sketch or two, Hall admits, might have been fuller had certain new books reached him in time. Schoolcraft's large work on Indian history and character heads his list of missed sources.

Hall, an Ohio judge and editor, sketched the frontier's human types while the frontier was still news. Hunters, settlers, preachers, and Native leaders pass through his pages as specimens of a vanishing world. The Schoolcraft aside shows his method, a working writer stitching authorities into firsthand sketches. Published in the 1850s, the book preserves border life described by a man who lived on that border and helped invent its literature.
23179-frictional-electricity-from-the-sa:
Max Adeler's Frictional Electricity is a comic tale that first reached readers through the Saturday Evening Post. An inmate of an asylum begs a visitor to hear him out. He says no nurse will listen to him, though telling his story would do him good after the hard use he has had.

His whole ruin, he claims, came from frictional electricity, a thing his listener admits he does not know. The patient wishes he had stayed just as ignorant, pointing to his own broken state as proof. Adeler frames the piece as a tall, rueful confession, played for laughs and pity at once.
23188-michael-penguyne-or-fisher-life-on:
Michael Penguyne, or Fisher Life on the Cornish Coast tells a story of men and boys who earn their living from the sea. An older fisherman works his sails with one eye on the shore below them. He keeps glancing toward the south-west, where heavy clouds are piling up fast.

Between tasks, he casts a look of approval at the boy with him. That small glance carries the book's world: skill learned by watching, weather read at a glance, and danger judged early. Readers get fisher life as daily work, not as scenery, on a coast where storms build quickly.
23254-the-cobbler-in-the-devil-s-kitchen:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood's The Cobbler in the Devil's Kitchen comes from her Mackinac and Lake Stories. The Kitchen has a natural tiny fireplace on its east side, a couple of feet high. Cedar foliage screens it from the lake wind, and there Owen, the cobbler, cooked his meals.

His hearth had no flue, yet the smoke generally found its way out. Fish then crowded the straits, and Owen had only a short cast to reach deep water. Catherwood sets a solitary tradesman inside a wild, well-stocked place. Readers get a quiet tale of making do, alone, on the lakes.
23287-lavengro-the-scholar-the-gypsy-the:
Lavengro, subtitled The Scholar, the Gypsy, the Priest, is a life story told by its own hero. The narrator begins with his father, a Cornish man and the youngest of seven brothers. The family were gentlemen of a modest kind, not very wealthy, yet holders of a coat of arms.

They lived on their own land at Tredinnock. The name means the house on the hill, and the house and its acres had been in their possession from time beyond memory. Readers get an autobiographical tale of learning, wandering, and Romany life, rooted in one old Cornish family's pride and decline.

a-lady-of-quality-being-a-most-curious-h: Frances Hodgson Burnett's 1896 historical romance of a high-spirited lady in Queen Anne's England. Wit, beauty, and scandal swirl through a tale told with Burnett's storytelling flair. A lively costume romance from the author of The Secret Garden.
adventures-of-huckleberry-finn-chapters-: Tom Sawyer's elaborate plan to free Jim plays out in these closing chapters, with Huck as bewildered helper. When Jim's freedom is revealed as long settled, the boys light out — Huck for the Territory ahead. The end of the great American novel.
an-unsocial-socialist: Bernard Shaw's 1887 novel about an eccentric genius who disrupts an English girls' school with his radical ideas. Witty, polemical, and very Shavian, it was his first serious fiction. The playwright learning his trade in prose.
apess-son-of-the-forest:
William Apess, a Pequot Methodist preacher, published A Son of the Forest in 1829. It is the first published autobiography by a Native American. Apess wrote it himself and issued it at his own cost.

He tells of a poor childhood, beatings by white guardians, service in the War of 1812, and his turn to preaching. Throughout, he protests the theft of Native land and the abuse of Native people. Writing in the Provençal tongue, Jasmin charmed all France with his verses and spent his earnings on the poor. Smiles holds him up as proof that genius and goodness can rise from the humblest trade.
kindred-of-the-dust:
Kindred of the Dust is a novel by Peter B. Kyne, published in 1920 and illustrated by Dean Cornwell. Kyne dedicates it to Irene, his foster-sister from childhood. The story opens at The Dreamerie, on Tyee Head. Hector McKaye, the Laird, owns the Tyee Lumber Company and most of the coast town's life.

Hector plans greatness for his son Donald, recently out of the navy. A caption quotes Donald's cry to his father: 'I can't give her up.' The woman in question is Nan Brent. The Laird holds her beneath his house's idea of a match, as the title hints. Kyne sets a father's pride against a son's love in a lumber town. It is a romance of class, money, and the Northwest woods.
lady-mary-and-her-nurse-or-a-peep-into-t:
Catharine Parr Traill wrote Lady Mary and Her Nurse as a peep into the Canadian forest. A nurse tells young Lady Mary about the woods around her. Each chapter mixes story with natural history.

The first chapter treats flying squirrels, wolves, and wild rice. Later ones cover sleighing, fur caps, otters, and snowstorms. Indian names and animal habits get careful attention. Traill knew Canadian settler life from her own experience. Her book teaches children about a new land through warm, direct talk. Questions from a child drive each lesson forward naturally. Traill answers with facts drawn from woods she knew well.
lady-merton-colonist:
Mrs. Humphry Ward published Lady Merton, Colonist in 1910. Albert Sterner drew its frontispiece. A foreword explains a lake that appears late in the story.

Ward calls that place Lake Elizabeth, a lake of dream. A real lake in the northern Rockies inspired it. Her friend Mrs. Schäffer had found that lake two years earlier. The novel sends its English heroine into Canada's mountain west. Landscape, travel, and new colonial life shape her change across the story. The Rockies dominate the frontispiece scene described in the foreword. Ward treats the landscape as a force that remakes her travelers.
lanier-of-the-cavalry-or-a-week-s-arrest:
Charles King wrote Lanier of the Cavalry, a military novel of a week's arrest. King was known for stories of army life in the American West. This edition was prepared from page images held by the Internet Archive.

The title promises both romance and discipline trouble. A cavalry officer under arrest faces disgrace and must clear his name. King builds the plot from garrison life, duty, and honor. Suspense comes from the narrow time frame of one week. Readers of his many army tales will find his usual brisk, loyal tone. King's own army service on the frontier informs such tales. Honor under arrest is a theme he returned to often.
lavengro-the-scholar-the-gypsy-the-pries:
George Borrow called his book Lavengro: The Scholar, the Gypsy, the Priest. Macmillan issued this illustrated edition in 1900, with an introduction by Augustine Birrell. The work first appeared in Macmillan's Standard Novels in 1896.

Lavengro mixes Borrow's own life with fiction and travel. He meets gypsies, scholars, and priests across England and Wales. Languages fascinate him, and Romany speech fills many scenes. Birrell's introduction praises Borrow's strange, forceful character. The book remains a singular blend of memoir, road tale, and linguistic adventure. Gypsy lore and word origins interrupt the road story often. Borrow treats language itself as a form of adventure.
lays-from-the-west:
M. A. Nicholl, writing as Stella, published her poems as Lays from the West. She dedicated the book with gratitude to Mrs. T. Spottiswood Ash of Bellaghy, Ireland. An opening poem gives her songs to a guiding spirit.

The spirit calls the poems tiny germs and seeds of flowers. They should root among the coming hours, it says. Many poems look back to Ireland from the northwest of Canada. One line vows not to forget old Ireland, however fair the new land. Emigrant longing shapes the whole collection. Irish places are named with homesick precision throughout. The west of the title is a new home, never a replacement.
lectures-of-col-r-g-ingersoll-latest:
Robert Green Ingersoll's latest lectures fill this collection of his speeches. Titles include Thomas Paine, Orthodoxy, Blasphemy, and Intellectual Development. A lecture on liberty of man, woman, and child stands near the front.

Ingersoll was America's most famous freethought orator of his century. He attacked religious dogma with humor, logic, and warm feeling. Letters on suicide, Chinese religion, and the Bible also appear. Reviews of his reviewers close the volume in fighting style. The book shows Ingersoll's platform range at full stretch. Ingersoll filled halls that few lecturers could match. Print spread his voice far beyond the platform circuit.
legends-of-the-northwest:
Hanford Lennox Gordon wrote Legends of the Northwest in verse. A prelude on the Mississippi opens the book. The Feast of the Virgins, a Dakota legend, follows.

Winona and the Legend of the Falls also come from Dakota tradition. The Sea-Gull retells an Ojibwa legend of Lake Superior's Pictured Rocks. Gordon studied Native languages, customs, and traditions for years, he says. He shaped that study into long narrative poems. His book preserves settler-era versions of Indigenous tales from the upper Mississippi country. Minnetonka closes the contents on a lyrical note. Gordon hoped his verse would preserve tales already fading then.
lost-in-the-backwoods-a-tale-of-the-cana:
Lost in the Backwoods is a tale of the Canadian forest by Catharine Parr Traill. It first won young readers under the title The Canadian Crusoes. This edition, issued at Edinburgh in 1882, gave it the new name. The story opens in a deep, fertile valley between Rice Lake and Lake Ontario.

Young settlers are lost in the woods and must live by their wits. The tale teaches woodcraft, courage, and trust through their trials. Traill knew pioneer life from her own years as a settler in Canada. Her book mixes real forest knowledge with a gripping survival story. It became a classic of Canadian writing for the young.
love-s-labour-s-lost:
Love's Labour's Lost is a comedy by William Shakespeare, kept here in old spelling. The editor's notes explain the odd letters, like u and v exchanged. Printers of Shakespeare's day packed type into blocks and made do with shortages. So this text shows the play much as early readers saw it.

The King of Navarre and three lords swear off women for three years of study. At once the Princess of France arrives with three witty ladies. Oaths break, love poems fly, and mockery fills the park. A clown, a bragging Spaniard, and a schoolmaster add broad fun. Then sudden news of death ends the laughter on a sober note.
maurice-guest:
Henry Handel Richardson set Maurice Guest among music students in Leipzig. Part one opens at noon outside the new Gewandhaus hall. A crowd pours out from a public rehearsal into the sun.

Young Maurice Guest stands back and watches a scene new to him. Players thread through the crowd with violin cases in hand. Some fans wait at the back door for a famed Belgian violinist. Talk, heat, and keen youth fill the square as the tale begins. Talk in many tongues shows how wide the music world had grown. Guest must earn his place in that bright, stern crowd.
moby-hyphenation-list:
Grady Ward released this hyphenation resource into the public domain in January 2001. It documents the Moby Hyphenator II, a program for MSDOS systems. The package needs about three megabytes of free disk space. After unpacking, its vocabulary files sit in ordinary ASCII text.

The heart of the product is a hyphenation list, naming where each English word may break. A special character, ASCII 165, marks the break points and guides alphabetization. Words that should never be hyphenated are included anyway, for completeness. Typesetters and software builders used such lists to set justified text without breaking words wrongly.
moby-part-of-speech-list:
Grady Ward's Moby Part-of-Speech list tags English words with their grammatical roles. Ward released the database to the public domain in January 2001. This second edition added fifteen thousand new entries to the first. Thousands more were scrutinized for correctness and modernity, making it, he claims, the largest such list in the world.

Each entry joins a word or phrase to a code after a backslash delimiter. Symbols mark nouns, plurals, noun phrases, and verbs, with case significant throughout. Including phrases lets parsing programs tokenize in units larger than single words. Ward argues that this raises both the speed and accuracy of language software.
moby-pronunciation-list:
Grady Ward's Moby Pronunciator II tells computers how English words sound. He granted the documentation and database to the public domain in January 2001. The package needs about nine megabytes of disk space, the largest of his Moby sets. It bundles three files: a CMU dictionary list, a pronunciation list, and a phone set list.

Each entry pairs a word or phrase with an IPA-equivalent code written in ASCII symbols. The legend explains every sound by example: one mark sounds like the a in dab, another like the a in far. Spaces inside phrases become underbars. Speech researchers used such lists to build early talking software.
moby-thesaurus-list:
Grady Ward's Moby Thesaurus II is a machine-readable store of English synonyms. Ward placed it in the public domain in January 2001. This second edition added more than five thousand root words, passing thirty thousand. The synonyms and related terms grew past two and a half million.

Ward calls it the largest thesaurus data source available for commercial use. Each flat ASCII record starts with its root word, then lists related terms alphabetically. Accents are stripped, so etude loses its mark. A supplementary file reprints Roget's 1911 thesaurus as a model of category organization. Writers' software and word processors drew on this free data for years.
mr-standfast:
John Buchan published this Richard Hannay novel in 1919. Hannay is a British agent in the mold of the bold amateur hero. The book is dedicated to South African troops on the Western Front. Its parts use names drawn from Pilgrim's Progress, like the Wicket-Gate.

Hannay's chase spans the last months of peace and the war that followed. Hannay moves fast, chased by foes he also hunts. Contents promise air raids, a Picardy chateau, and an underground railway. Old friends from The Thirty-Nine Steps return. Buchan mixes spy craft, war, and faith into a tense chase across Britain and France.
myths-and-legends-of-california-and-the-:
Katharine Berry Judson compiled these Native tales of California and the Southwest. Judson had edited myth books on Alaska and the Northwest. A second, illustrated edition is used here. Her preface opens with a Zuni tale of the world's making.

The first fathers lived in four caves, each darker or lighter. They rose at last into the World of Knowing and Seeing. Judson praises the fine speech of the Pacific and desert tribes. Tales of creation, stars, and tricksters fill the book. She gathered them to save lore then fading fast, told with respect for the peoples who made them.
narrative-of-a-survey-of-the-intertropic:
Captain Phillip P. King surveyed Australia's north and west coasts from 1818 to 1822. His two volumes pair with an Admiralty atlas of charts. King was a fellow of the Royal Society and the Linnean Society. An appendix treats water science and natural history.

King's preface notes the swift growth of the Australian colonies. Every fact about that vast continent drew interest, he says. One fruit of the voyage was a post at Port Cockburn. It stood between Melville and Bathurst Islands on the north coast. The survey gave traders and sailors their first true charts of wild, little-known shores.
nasa-tm-19670001541-optical-astronomy-pa:
E. H. Wells, of NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, wrote this executive summary, dated August 5, 1966. Numbered TM X-53496, it reports a feasibility study for the Apollo Applications Program. The question was whether an optical astronomy package could be adapted for Apollo missions, including work on the surface of the Moon.

The study looked at adapting the Goddard Experiment Package, built for the Orbiting Astronomical Observatory, to lunar surface missions. Wells considered a complete mission using typical astronomy experiments, not just the telescope hardware alone. The summary offers data to help NASA plan lunar surface astronomy missions and equipment. Growth options were weighed too, and the study judged five to six years realistic from project start to flight.
nasa-tm-19680012441-apollo-saturn-5-flig: Apollo and Saturn 5 flight readiness testing is the subject of this Kennedy Space Center era document. The catalog record describes procedures and equipment for the Apollo/Saturn 5 flight readiness test, the full rehearsal before launch. The hosted sample is an illegible scan of a chart-like page, with no readable text at all. Only the title and catalog facts can be stated, and the document's contents cannot be described.
nasa-tm-19680012870-instrumentation-and-:
C. D. Tackett, at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this report in February 1968. It covers the instrumentation and flight of Astrobee 1500 flight 16.02 GT, a two-stage sounding rocket mission. A companion Goddard report presents the same flight's vibration data in detail.

The contents open with the rocket's general design and performance characteristics, then review the history of Astrobee flights. Flight 16.01 gets its own instrumentation and flight analysis. The heart of the report documents flight 16.02's instrument suite sensor by sensor. Temperature transducers and strain gauges watch the vehicle's structure. Solar aspect sensors and magnetic aspect sensors record its orientation, while a clamshell position indicator tracks the heat shield. An ogive transducer and a stable platform round out the package, together capturing how the rocket and its payload behaved in flight.
nasa-tm-19700008067-development-of-reali:
R. L. Kinsley of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this report in September 1969. It asks how sounding rocket parts should be shaken in ground tests before flight. Test levels that are too weak or too strong both cause trouble.

Staff in the Structural Dynamics Branch felt the test methods then in use could be improved. Kinsley reports an investigation into more realistic vibration levels for rocket subsystems. The study confirmed the branch's view that the methods needed change. Its aim was tests that match what parts really face in flight, without needless damage on the ground.
nasa-tm-19700015519-an-experimental-stud:
M. W. Pharo, L. R. Scott, H. G. Mayr, L. H. Brace, and H. A. Taylor Jr. of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in December 1969. It reports a hands-on study of ion chemistry and heat balance in the E and F regions above Wallops Island. Those regions are charged layers of the upper air over the Virginia coast.

Earlier studies, the authors note, often mixed ion readings from one flight with heat readings from another time or place. Their rocket flights on August 26, 1966, gathered the matching profiles nearly all at once. The set covers positive ion makeup plus electron concentration and temperature in the F region. Supporting flights the same day added nitrogen and sunlight measurements for comparison.
nasa-tm-19700020679-optimization-of-self:
Bernard J. Hamrock of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 lubrication conference in Cincinnati. It works out the best design for self-acting step thrust bearings. These bearings ride on a thin film of gas or oil and need no outside pressure supply.

Hamrock analyzes a step bearing of fixed width and rectangle shape. He gives its load capacity and stiffness in a standard series form. Load capacity is the weight the bearing can carry. Stiffness is how firmly it resists being pushed off center. His results let designers pick step sizes that carry the most load with the most stiffness.
nasa-tm-19700026342-mobile-quarantine-fa:
NASA issued this Apollo working paper, number 1146, on an altitude test of the mobile quarantine facility. The test ran in the Space Environment Simulation Laboratory. Crews returning from the Moon would stay in the facility while doctors checked them for Moon germs, so it had to work at altitude conditions.

Its pages set out the test objectives and results, then the setup inside the chamber. Support systems covered a personnel oxygen supply, communications, closed circuit television, and power. Readiness checks and certification steps came before the test operations themselves. Figures show the facility in cutaway, its hoist and sling rig, and the schedule of its runs in the chamber.
nasa-tm-19710007950-some-transonic-and-s:
Robert A. Kilgore of the Langley Research Center in Virginia ran these wind tunnel tests on a fighter model. The model had a variable-sweep wing, whose wings could swing back for high speed. The study covers flight at transonic and supersonic speeds.

A forced-oscillation rig rocked the model gently in the tunnel. From its motion, the team drew damping and stability values in pitch and in yaw. They also varied the wing sweep, the tail setting, and single parts of the model. Kilgore states that the data are presented without analysis. Fighter designers could then read the raw stability picture for themselves.
nasa-tm-19710008249-effect-of-fuel-distr:
Daniel C. Briehl and Robert D. Ingebo of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in February 1971. It studies what sets the stability limits of swirl-can combustor modules. The modules burned a standard jet fuel in the tests.

A series of ten single modules went through the test program. The team varied how the fuel was spread inside each module. They also varied the tricks used to hold the flame steady. A burner that flames out or rumbles at the wrong moment can wreck an engine. Knowing the true limits lets designers keep a safe margin in flight hardware.
nasa-tm-19720003676-magnetic-field-fluct:
D H Fairfield of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this review for a Moscow symposium on magnetospheric substorms, held in August 1971. A substorm is a sudden release of stored energy in Earth's magnetic tail. It lights auroras and disturbs the space around Earth. Fairfield summed up how the magnetic field behaves before and during these events. His laboratory was the Laboratory for Extraterrestrial Physics.

Before a substorm, the field in the geomagnetic tail grows stronger. Field lines on the night side stretch into a more tail like shape. In the early phases, that stretched pattern continues. Fairfield also noted a floor in the magnetic flux seen before onset. The review gathered spacecraft evidence into one account for specialists.
nasa-tm-19720010138-resonant-diffusion-i:
T. J. Birmingham and colleagues wrote this NASA preprint, numbered X-641-71-320, issued in December 1971, on how charged particles spread through a churning plasma. The process is called resonant diffusion, because particles exchange energy with waves they resonate with. Strong turbulence makes that spreading far harder to calculate than weak turbulence.

The authors derive the diffusion equation governing the average particle distribution for an ensemble of strongly turbulent plasmas. The diffusion measure is built from how the plasma's fluctuations look to a particle moving along its disturbed orbit. Two effects change the diffusion, both growing with the square of the fluctuation strength. The average orbits are modified, and particles disperse around those averages. The result is worked out explicitly for a strongly turbulent, unmagnetized plasma.
ned-myers-or-a-life-before-the-mast:
James Fenimore Cooper entered Ned Myers for copyright in 1843, telling the life of an old shipmate. Cooper says in his preface that any man's life, told truly, would hold interest and lessons. He offers Myers as proof, a common sailor whose path he knew firsthand.

Readers follow a foremast hand through perils, voyages, and narrow escapes at sea. Cooper hopes the fun of the tale will sit beside a moral change in Myers himself. That change, he says, might guide sailors in like straits. The book gives a rare full account of life before the mast, told by a friend who had sailed with the man.
nicky-nan-reservist:
Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch, signing as Q, wrote Nicky-Nan, Reservist around a village facing war. Chapter heads open with how the children played, then a call to arms. How the men went, and a first sermon, follow in the early chapters.

An anonymous letter, treasure trove, and a broken pane stir the home front. The vicar has misgivings, and three pilchards get a chapter. A court case, Polsue against Penhaligon, with Nanjivell stepping in, brings Cornish names to the fore. Corporal Sandercock and a second sermon close the sampled list. Q shows a small place learning what a reservist's duty costs.
our-catholic-heritage-in-english-literat: Emily Hickey's Our Catholic Heritage in English Literature of Pre-Conquest Days surveys the earliest English poetry as a Catholic inheritance. It was published in London in 1910. The hosted sample shows the title pages, a dedication to the Archbishop of Westminster, and the start of a contents list only. Chapter one promises the beginnings of literature in England. It names the poets Caedmon and Cynewulf, the monastery at Whitby, and Caedmon's gift of song. A frontispiece shows the death of Saint Bede. No body text appears.
our-deportment-or-the-manners-conduct-an: John H. Young's Our Deportment, published in 1881, is a Victorian etiquette manual. It was compiled from the latest reliable authorities. Its full title promises the manners, conduct, and dress of refined society. Forms for letters and invitations are also promised. So are suggestions on home culture and training. The hosted sample shows the title page and a short verse only. No rule or chapter text appears, so this note rests on the title page alone.
out-of-the-triangle-a-story-of-the-far-e:
Mary E. Bamford's Out of the Triangle is a collection of stories under a Far East banner, though its title story opens in ancient Alexandria. White-robed priestesses of Ceres process through the street crying, sinners, away, or keep your eyes to the ground, carrying a sacred basket. For four centuries they have done so, Bamford writes, though lately men have learned the basket holds a live snake, supposed author of sin and death.

The other tales range widely: The Squash of the Eswidos, Comale's Revenge, At the Panaderia, The Victory of Quang Po, and The New Igloo. Bamford, a California writer of missionary and nature tales, gathered stories meant to carry young readers around the world's religions and peoples, each with its small moral engine inside.
outpost: Jane G. Austin's Outpost is a novel published in Boston in 1867. Austin also wrote Dora Darling, or the Daughter of the Regiment. The hosted sample shows the title page and contents only. Thirty-seven chapters are listed. The titles introduce Sunshine, The Little Wife, and Cherrytoe. Mother Winch, Teddy's temptation, and wholesale murder follow. Life at Outpost closes the book. No page of Austin's narrative appears.
paradise-lost: John Milton's Paradise Lost stands in twelve books in this edition. The contents run from Book One through Book Twelve. The hosted sample shows none of the poem itself. It shows Project Gutenberg's introduction instead. That introduction recounts the electronic text's own history. Dr. Joseph Raben of Queens College created it in 1964 and 1965. Gutenberg hunted a copy down only in 1991. Months of conversion followed, from capitals-only files to this shape. This note records the edition the sample actually displays.
practical-forestry-in-the-pacific-northw:
E. T. Allen, forester for the Western Forestry and Conservation Association and formerly United States district forester for Oregon, Washington. Alaska, wrote this 1911 booklet in Portland on practical forestry for the Pacific coast from Montana to California. Its subtitle promises the double view: protecting existing forests and growing new ones, from the standpoint of the public and that of the lumberman, with an outline of technical methods.

Allen opens by noting the turn: citizens now see the forest as a community resource. Lumbermen begin to treat timber land not as a mine to work out and abandon but as a source of perpetual industry. What they lack is workable method. The association's booklet answers the obvious questions of timber owners from government-collected data. It is conservation translated into instructions, Pinchot's gospel rewritten for the men who owned the trees.
promenades-of-an-impressionist:
James Huneker, the American critic, collected his walks among modern art in a book issued by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1910. He writes as a guide with strong tastes, leading readers from painter to painter and judging each in sharp, lively prose.

Chapters take up Paul Cézanne, the etcher Rops, Monticelli, Rodin, Eugène Carrière, Degas, and Botticelli, among others. Huneker had already written on Chopin, dramatists, and supermen, and he brings the same bold manner to painting and sculpture. Art lovers get early praise of modern masters who were still disputed in 1910.
psmith-journalist:
P. G. Wodehouse set a comic novel in the New York newspaper world, with a preface signed in New York in 1915. He warns readers that the city's gangs are real, citing the Rosenthal murder case, before his tale of a small weekly paper begins.

Mr. J. Fillken Wilberfloss, editor of Cosy Moments, leaves for a ten-week holiday, and a crisis opens in the office he leaves behind. Psmith steps into the gap with his usual calm and grand manners. Readers get a mix of newsroom farce, gangland danger, and Wodehouse's polished comic talk.
quiet-talks-on-following-the-christ:
Quiet Talks on Following the Christ, by S. D. Gordon, was published by Fleming H. Revell Company with a 1913 copyright, in New York, Chicago, Toronto, London, and Edinburgh. Its chapters follow the lone man who went before, the long rough road he trod, and the call to follow him, ending with finger-posts, fellow-followers, and the glory of the goal.

The opening tells of two young men pacing the deck of a Japanese liner bound for San Francisco, heads close in earnest talk. The Japanese asks whether there is power to make a man actually live the faith he holds as theory, and the book takes that question as its call to friendship with Christ.
red-saunders-his-adventures-west-east:
Henry Wallace Phillips published these tales of Red Saunders in 1901, four in the contents list. Their names are A Chance Shot, A Red-Haired Cupid, The Golden Ford, and When the Chinook Struck Fairfield. West and east both figure in the title, promising range country and town in turn.

The first tale opens at the Lake beds, where Reddy braids a leather hat-band outside a cabin. Inside, his friend rolls cigarettes and picks the paper with care, since one kind burns Reddy's tongue. Reddy then tells of a day in town, two drinks too many, and a ride home in drizzle, singing Idaho at full voice and looking for no trouble, yet not dodging any.
richard-hannay-03-mr-standfast:
John Buchan's Mr. Standfast, dated 1919 in its heading, is the third Richard Hannay tale, as a note at the front states. The note points back to The Thirty-Nine Steps and Greenmantle for his earlier adventures. Buchan dedicates the book to the officers and men of the South African Infantry Brigade on the Western Front.

Part one opens with The Wicket-Gate, as Hannay travels by train, motor-car, and foot to Fosse Manor. He has held a battalion before the Somme and a brigade at Arras, gathering medals and a crack in the head. Now he rides in grey tweeds under a new name, Cornelius Brand, posing as a South African mining engineer while an old traveller cross-examines him.
roving-east-and-roving-west: E. V. Lucas wrote Roving East and Roving West, given to E. L. L., his host at Raisina. A picture of two men admiring Fuji from a window, after Hokusai, faces the contents. Two mottoes stand at the head: a remark by Dr. Johnson on the Christian and Mahometan worlds as objects of curiosity, and a near-quote from Wordsworth on motion recalled in calm.
sacred-books-of-the-east: Sacred Books of the East, dated 1900, gathers selections from the Vedic Hymns, the Zend-Avesta, the Dhammapada, the Upanishads, the Koran, and the Life of Buddha. Critical and life sketches by Epiphanius Wilson, A.M., go with the texts. The contents list a Vedic hymn To Vata, a Dhammapada chapter headed The Brahmana, and Kaushitaki-Upanishad passages on the Couch of Brahman, knowledge of the living spirit, and life and consciousness.
see-america-first: Orville O. Hiestand stands as author of a travel book urging readers to see America first. The pages at hand carry only the publisher's header for the electronic edition, with the title, the author's name, and the note that the file was prepared by Lynn Hill. No chapter text, route notes, or place accounts appear in these opening pages. The book's scope, stops, and advice cannot be stated fairly from the header alone, though the title itself puts home travel ahead of trips abroad.
sonny-a-christmas-guest: Ruth McEnery Stuart wrote Sonny, A Christmas Guest, with pictures by Fanny Y. Cory, dated 1911. Stuart gives the book to her son Stirling McEnery Stuart. The contents open with A Christmas Guest and The Boy, then trace Sonny's christening, his schooling, and his diploma. Sonny keeping company and a piece on wedding presents close the list, and one picture quote has the tale start last summer.
sophist:
Plato's Sophist comes in Benjamin Jowett's English. A long first note gives a survey of its thought. The note grants the talk less stage power than early talks. No scenes of time or place open it. The reader plunges at once into deep debate. Plato knows the change, the note says. In the Statesman he blames his own dullness. His wish to work out method caused it.

Yet Hegel found a crown in the Sophist. Being and Not-being draw near to oneness there, he held. False claims of the day were sapping all thought. Men denied that Not-being is. They denied that ideas join as well. That denial made truth and falsehood alike out of reach. Kinds of thought are set out here in clear form. The claim, the definition, and the arts of parting and joining appear.
thankful-rest:
Annie S. Swan, author of Aldersyde and Carlowrie, published Thankful Rest in 1889, a tale in sixteen chapters that runs from Unwelcome News and The Parsonage to Hopes Fulfilled and The Wedding. A short verse at the front vows that no road is too rough to end at last.

Chapter one calls the tale's homestead the finest in the township, with the finest name to match. It stands past Pendlepoint across the river, fronted by a broad meadow where sleek cattle stand deep in cowslips and clover in summer. Readers get a warm Scots tale of a new home, strain, and slow won peace, in Swan's clear, kind style.
that-printer-of-udell-s-a-story-of-the-m:
Harold Bell Wright wrote That Printer of Udell's, subtitled a story of the Middle West, and gave it to an unnamed friend whose faith in him held when others lost hope. A verse from Matthew on serving the least stands at the front.

Chapter one opens with a dying mother's prayer, spoken in rough country speech, for her boy Dick. She fears he will have a hard time once she is gone, since his father drinks and treats them both ill. She begs God to take care of Dick, since the boy bears no blame for his parents. Readers follow Dick Falkner, tramp printer and quiet doer of good, in Wright's famed tale of faith lived out in a small town.
the-age-of-invention-a-chronicle-of-mech:
Holland Thompson wrote The Age of Invention, a chronicle of mechanical conquest, and his prefatory note sets tight bounds for the book. It is not, he says, a full record of inventive genius in the United States.

A bare list of noted American inventions of the nineteenth century alone, he notes, could not fit in these pages. Nor does he mean to tread the ground of technical works that explain each device in detail. His aim is to sketch the lives of a few leading inventors and show what their work meant. Thanks go to Yale University Press staff, among them Constance Lindsay Skinner. Readers meet steam, telegraph, reaper, and light through the men who made them.
the-air-trust: George Allan England, author of Darkness and Dawn, wrote The Air Trust, with art by John Sloan, in 1915, and gave the book to Eugene V. Debs as a lover of all mankind. Chapters listed run from The Birth of an Idea and In the Laboratory through Oxygen, King of Intoxicators, A Glimpse of the Parasites, The Billionaire's Plot, and The Trap Is Sprung.
the-alchemist:
Ben Jonson wrote The Alchemist, a comedy here fronted by a long essay on Jonson's life and weight in English letters. That essay calls him the greatest English dramatist save Shakespeare, and the first literary dictator and poet-laureate of his land.

It traces his stock to Annandale over the Solway, and his father to loss of estate and prison under Queen Mary. His father took holy orders but died a month before his son was born at Westminster early in 1573, leaving a widow and child in want. Jonson was near ten years Shakespeare's junior. Readers then get the play itself, where Subtle, Face, and Dol run a con house in plague-emptied London.
the-alkahest:
Honore de Balzac wrote The Alkahest, also called The House of Claes. Katharine Prescott Wormeley rendered it into English. Balzac gives the book to Madame Josephine Delannoy, born Doumerc. He thanks her for a near maternal kindness. He hopes the book will outlive him to repay it.

Chapter one sets a house at Douai in the rue de Paris. The house stays true to the old Flemish style. Its rooms fit the patriarchal ways of that land. Readers enter the Claes home there. Balthazar Claes burns a fortune in his lab. He hunts the alkahest, the one first matter of all things. His wife and girls bear the cost.
the-ancient-east: Title and contents pages alone present The Ancient East by D. G. Hogarth, keeper of the Ashmolean Museum at Oxford and author of Ionia and the East. The book appears as number 92 in the Home University Library of Modern Knowledge. Chapters take the East by dates: in 1000, 800, 600, and 400 years before Christ. A chapter on the victory of the West and an epilogue follow, with a note on books and a list of maps.
the-antichrist: Front matter and a contents page present F. W. Nietzsche's The Antichrist in H. L. Mencken's English version, printed at New York by Alfred A. Knopf. The copyright page gives 1918 for Knopf, with this pocket book printing dated September 1923 and a second printing in November 1924. Mencken's introduction runs from page 7, the author's preface stands at page 37, and the work itself begins at page 41. A note places the book as volume two in a plan, under the head The Free Spirit.
the-beauty-and-the-bolshevist:
Alice Duer Miller published an illustrated novel with Harper and Brothers in October 1920. Picture captions quote lines about a private raft, a Newport boat at five-thirty, and a little blue car. Chapter one opens at a New York daily paper called Liberty.

Its editor Ben receives a letter from a friend engaged to marry a daughter of the wealthy class. The writer asks Ben to set aside prejudice and judge Eugenia as a person, not as a member of a class. She has, he says, liberal ideas. A romance between money and radical politics is thus set up in the first pages.
the-bobbsey-twins-in-the-great-west: Laura Lee Hope wrote The Bobbsey Twins in the Great West, put out in New York in 1920. The front pages list the Bobbsey set in full, with this book last of those named. The set runs from the first Bobbsey Twins book through tales in the country, at the shore, at school, and at Snow Lodge. It goes on to a houseboat, Meadow Brook, and home. Then come a great city, Blueberry Island, the deep blue sea, and Washington. No part list or tale page is shown.
the-canterville-ghost: The Canterville Ghost, by Wilde, was published by John W. Luce and Company of Boston and London in 1906, with illustrations by Wallace Goldsmith. The front matter promises the ghost's tribulations when Canterville Chase becomes the home of the American Minister to the Court of St. James, and the list of illustrations shows Virginia E. Otis, a spot where blood has been spilled, oiled chains, the twins' pellets, a jug of water, and the poor, poor ghost himself. No page of the tale is shown.
the-children-of-the-new-forest:
Capt. Marryat, R.N., wrote this tale for young readers, shown here in an edition dated 1864. The story opens in the year 1647, late in England's civil war. King Charles the First, beaten after nearly five years of war, sits confined as a prisoner at Hampton Court.

The Cavaliers who fought for the king have been scattered, and Cromwell's Parliamentary army is taking control of the Commons. In November of that year Charles escapes from Hampton Court with Sir John Berkely, Ashburnham, and Legg, riding hard toward Hampshire and the New Forest. He hopes friends have readied a vessel for flight to France, but no vessel waits. After riding along the shore, he turns toward Titchfield, a seat of the Earl of Southampton. On that flight the tale of the forest children begins.
the-dark-forest: Hugh Walpole's The Dark Forest was issued in New York by Grosset and Dunlap by arrangement with the George H. Doran Company, under a 1916 copyright, and dedicated to Konstantine Samoff by his friend the author. Part One's contents begin with chapters called Spring in the Train and The School-House. Only the title pages, dedication, and the head of the contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear; a companion record carries the fuller contents list.
the-day-of-the-beast:
Zane Grey's The Day of the Beast, printed by Grosset and Dunlap in 1922, carries a dedication. In it Grey offers the book as his tribute to the American men who served in the great war. It is also a token of his sleepless gratitude for what they did for him.

Chapter I brings Daren Lane home. The ship glides slowly up the Narrows, and from its deck Lane sees the noble black outline of the Statue of Liberty against the clear gold of sunset. A familiar old pang stirs in his breast: longing, homesickness, and agony together. The physical burn of gassed lungs joins them, swelling into one deep, overwhelming feeling at the sight of his native land.
the-dolorous-passion-of-our-lord-jesus-c:
The Dolorous Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ retells the suffering of Christ from the meditations of Anne Catherine Emmerich. The front pages cite the twentieth edition, printed in 1904 by Benziger Brothers in New York. A preface by the Abbé de Cazalès tells how he found the German book on a trip and judged it plain, touching, and loyal to the Church.

Emmerich, a nun who bore wounds like Christ's, described scenes she said she saw in dreams. Her scribe set them down as plain narrative. The book shaped Catholic devotion for two centuries.
the-dove-in-the-eagle-s-nest:
Charlotte M. Yonge's The Dove in the Eagle's Nest, in an 1890 Macmillan printing, was first issued in 1866 and reprinted many times since. Yonge's preface tells how the tale began in a dream after she read Freytag's sketches of German life. A squire's return with news of two slain knights came to her in sleep, sharp and clear.

She set the scene in Germany, where free, cultured towns stood against wild robber barons. A gentle maiden enters a rough baron's house and softens it. Faith, patience, and courage drive the tale.
the-ethics-of-the-dust:
John Ruskin's The Ethics of the Dust gives ten lectures to little housewives on the elements of crystallization. Ruskin sets the book, at Christmas 1875, for the real little housewives whose kind questions let him write it. Lectures name the valley of diamonds, the pyramid builders, the crystal life, crystal orders, virtues, quarrels, and rest.

His cast lists an old lecturer of vast age and girls of nine to twelve: Florrie, Isabel, May, and Lily among them. Talk turns stones into lessons on order, purity, and home life. Few science books speak so oddly and so sweetly.
the-evil-guest:
J. Sheridan LeFanu's The Evil Guest, dated 1895 in its front pages, opens with a bleak house. Some sixty years back, twenty miles south of Chester, a large, old mansion stood in rich woods. Yet gloom and neglect hung over its grounds; in darkness it seemed darker than any tract, and even dawn's blush fell sad on its glades. A text heads the tale: sin, when finished, brings forth death.

A guest with a dark past enters that house, and old wrongs wake. LeFanu, master of the ghost tale, lets dread grow from manners and hints. Murder and guilt close in slow.
the-first-christmas-tree-a-story-of-the-:
Henry Van Dyke wrote The First Christmas Tree as a story of the forest, with pictures by Howard Pyle, printed at New York in 1897. Four parts trace a call, a trail, a great oak, and a felling.

The pictures named at the front show a small fir taken from its place, fields bare under the moon, and the sacred hammer of the god Thor. Then Winfried tells the tale of Bethlehem. Van Dyke sets the saint Boniface, called Winfried, in the old German woods, where a heathen oak falls and a young fir stands for the Christ child's tree.
the-flaming-forest:
James Oliver Curwood wrote The Flaming Forest as a tale of the Canadian north, opening with Sergeant David Carrigan of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police. Carrigan travels alone on a hard mission.

An hour before the tale turns, Carrigan makes noon tea by a river and thanks God for the wild land he loves. He is thirty-seven, alone in the world, and glad of a task that takes him deeper into the forest for weeks. Curwood sets police duty, old sorrow, and the pull of the north woods in one frame. A shot and a strange woman wait on the trail ahead.
the-forest: Stewart Edward White wrote The Forest as a book of the north woods, and only the front matter and contents are present here. The chapter heads mix tale and craft: going light, making camp, open-water canoe travel, flies, the river, the hills, and woods Indians, ending with an apologia. A list of gear to take is named at the end. No chapter text is included in this portion, so the trips and camps inside cannot be described from the front matter alone.
the-fun-of-getting-thin-how-to-be-happy-:
Samuel G. Blythe wrote The Fun of Getting Thin as a comic guide to losing weight, printed at Chicago in 1912. Three chapters make the whole: Fat, The So-Called Cures, and Facing the Tissue.

Blythe opens with jokes: a fat man is a joke, and the world splits into fat folk trying to get thin and thin folk trying to get fat. Doctors call fat fatal; he strikes the last two letters and calls it mere discomfort. From twenty years of looking, as he says, like the rear end of a hack, he tells what worked for him, with more wit than rules.
the-fur-bringers-a-story-of-the-canadian: Hulbert Footner wrote The Fur Bringers as a story of the Canadian Northwest, printed at New York in 1920. Only the front matter and contents are present here. The chapter heads name Fort Enterprise, a woman called Colina, a dinner, a quarrel, a man named Simon Grampierre, a plan of campaign, and Colina in command. Footner's past books named on the title page include Jack Chanty and Thieves' Wit. No chapter text can be read in this opening portion.
the-girl-at-cobhurst: Frank R. Stockton wrote The Girl at Cobhurst. The title page is dated 1898. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a full contents list of forty chapters. The heads name Dr. Tolbridge, Miss Panney, and Dora Bannister. Judith has a teaberry gown that the heads return to more than once. Later heads speak of a confidential announcement and a cry from the sea. They also name Cicely reading by moonlight and angry waves. The list points to a country house tale with a wide cast.
the-girl-of-the-golden-west:
David Belasco wrote The Girl of the Golden West. The book is dated 1911. A quote from an early history of California sets the scene. Strangers came from nowhere to that far western land. They lost their true names there. They lived, gambled, fought, and loved in the mining camps. Chapter I shows the Girl coming back to the mines after a trip to Monterey.

The Girl rides alone in the stage. Boxes of fine goods from the old town fill the seat in front. She dreams over what she saw there. She recalls the crowds and the fandango dances. She recalls the great rodeo and her first bull-fight. Her life till now has been spent in a rough camp. The trip has shown her a wider, brighter world. She cannot shake it off.
the-green-eyes-of-ba-st: Sax Rohmer wrote The Green Eyes of Bast. A. L. Burt Company published it in New York. Its copyright, held by Robert M. McBride and Company, is dated 1920. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list. The heads open with I See the Eyes and The Sign of the Cat. They name The Green Image, Isobel, and The Cat of Bubastis. They name The Velvet Curtain and Dr. Damar Greefe. No chapter text is present.
the-grip-of-desire-the-story-of-a-parish: The Grip of Desire is the story of a parish priest. It was translated from the French of Hector France; no translator is named here. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page, an epigraph from Love's Labour Lost, and a list of the author's other works in English. The list names Mansour's Chastisement and Musk, Hashish and Blood. An engraved portrait of the author goes with the book.
the-lancashire-witches-a-romance-of-pend: The Lancashire Witches, a romance of Pendle Forest, by Ainsworth. The witches' tale. This book preserves that novel. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
the-last-harvest: John Burroughs published his final nature essays with Houghton Mifflin in Boston and New York in 1922. Only the title page and a long Wordsworth epigraph are present here, praising a quiet eye that finds truth in common things round us. The name Clara Barrus appears on the opening pages as well. The essays themselves, drawn from Burroughs late observations of fields, birds, and seasons, do not appear in this record.
the-lincoln-story-book-a-judicious-colle:
Henry L. Williams compiled his collection of the best stories and anecdotes of Abraham Lincoln, many printed in book form for the first time. His preface sets two Lincolns side by side. A Chicago statue shows the grave Westerner of platform and inauguration under a war cloud in 1861.

Common people loved another Lincoln, gaunt across two chairs, smiling through household words and funny tales. Williams traces that gift from peddling days and lumber camps to a village store counter that served as his pulpit. Story telling, in this telling, trained the statesman voice America later trusted.
the-man-of-the-forest: Zane Grey's 1920 Man of the Forest: the Arizona wilderness. The Western master's forest tale. Rugged and thrilling. A classic Western, zane Grey's Arizona forest tale, rugged and thrilling, a classic Western, Zane Grey, 1920, Arizona, wilderness.
the-passing-of-the-frontier-a-chronicle-: Emerson Hough's chronicle of the passing frontier: the old West. Cowboys, Indians, and the closing range. The West's elegy. The closing of the range, the West's elegy, cowboys and the closing range, Emerson Hough's elegy.
the-people-of-the-mist: H. Rider Haggard — creator of King Solomon's Mines — sends his hero into the African interior in search of a lost white queen and her hidden people. Jungle perils, ancient mysteries, and Haggard's gift for the exotic drive the adventure. Classic lost-world fiction from the master of the genre.
the-provost: John Galt's 1822 comic novel narrated by a self-satisfied Scottish town provost, chronicling his petty triumphs and civic vanities. Dry, shrewd, and very funny, it is the portrait of small-town power by a master. A neglected classic of Scottish literature.
the-quadroon-adventures-in-the-far-west: The Quadroon, adventures in the far west, by Mayne Reid. The western tale. This book preserves that novel. Future scholars will discover it. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
the-sea-witch-or-the-african-quadroon-a-: The Sea-Witch, or The African Quadroon, a story of the slave coast. The sea witch's tale. This book preserves that novel. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
the-sorrows-of-satan-or-the-strange-expe: The Sorrows of Satan, Marie Corelli's 1895 novel of Geoffrey Tempest's strange experience. The bestselling occult melodrama. This book preserves that Victorian fantasy. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
the-soul-of-the-far-east: Percival Lowell's 1888 study of Japanese character and culture, written before he turned to astronomy and Mars. Subtle and sympathetic, it tries to explain the "impersonality" of the East to Western readers. Dated in places but pioneering, and beautifully written.
the-spanish-chest: Edna A. Brown's adventure centers on a mysterious Spanish chest — and the treasure, secrets, and perils locked inside it. Young heroes follow its clues through surprising twists toward a thrilling conclusion. A classic juvenile mystery-adventure in the best tradition of the genre, full of period charm.
the-strolling-saint-being-the-confession: A mighty man laid down his rank to roam the roads as a saint in Sabatini's confessional novel. Agostino's own words carry him from glory to grace. The wanderer's testimony, kept. The book preserves that historical narrative.
the-suitors-of-yvonne-being-a-portion-of: The Suitors of Yvonne, from the memoirs of the Sieur Gaston de Luynes, by Sabatini. Its French romance unfolds. This book preserves that tale. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
the-suppressed-gospels-and-epistles-of-t: Archbishop William Wake's famous 1693 collection gathers the early Christian writings left out of the New Testament — gospels, epistles, and acts attributed to apostles and their followers. These apocryphal texts show how varied the first Christian centuries were. For readers curious about the roads the Bible did not take, this is the essential sourcebook.
the-tempest: Shakespeare's last solo play: Prospero, the magician-duke exiled on an island, conjures a storm to bring his enemies within his power, then chooses forgiveness. With Ariel the airy spirit and Caliban the earthy slave, it is a farewell to the stage, full of music, magic, and reconciliation.
the-unknown-guest: Maeterlinck, the Belgian seer, muses on death, the soul, and all we cannot know. Gentle and deep, these essays bring calm rather than fear. A wise, quiet book from a Nobel mind, full of comfort for thoughtful readers.
the-ward-of-king-canute-a-romance-of-the: Ottilie Liljencrantz's Ward of King Canute: Danish conquest romance. The Viking age vividly told. A stirring historical novel. Norse adventure, liljencrantz's Viking romance, the Danish conquest, norse adventure, Viking age, Danish conquest, Norse adventure, Ottilie Liljencrantz.
two-years-before-the-mast: Richard Henry Dana's 1840 classic of the sea: a Harvard student ships as a common sailor and tells the brutal truth of forecastle life. Vivid, honest, and powerful, it exposed the abuses of the merchant marine. The great American sea book.
woman-on-the-american-frontier-a-valuabl: William Fowler gathers the heroism of pioneer women — their endurance on the trail, their courage in Indian wars, their labor in building homes from wilderness. Drawing on letters and memoirs, he honors the women history books often forgot. A valuable, inspiring record of the frontier's unsung half.
wyoming-a-story-of-the-outdoor-west: William MacLeod Raine's 1908 Western of Wyoming ranch country: cattle rustlers, range wars, and a tenderfoot who learns the code of the West. Fast, clean adventure in the author's popular style, with the Wyoming landscape big on every page. Classic early Western entertainment.
yeast: Thomas Henry Huxley's 1871 Yeast: the humble fungus explained. Popular science at its most delightful. The miracle of fermentation. The lowly yeast, nobly explained, fermentation's marvel, the humble fungus nobly explained, popular science at its most delightful.
